rationale: The speech subtype study omitted the sialorrhea item. Its comparisons concern acoustic patterns and selected motor measures without raw figs.
The clinical treatment study measures salivary flow and patient drooling in neurological disease. It supplies symptom measurement context without a raw-fig exposure.

The study measures response to a medical intervention for chronic sialorrhea. Pain or discomfort appears as a generic quality-of-life item. The article provides no dried-date comparison or dedicated pain endpoint.
Pain is discussed as a possible barrier in a neurological rehabilitation pilot protocol. There is no measured date intervention or pain contrast.
The medication cohort reports 53 versus 37 participants with a pooled pain, anxiety and distress fluctuation item. The measure is a count and provides no dried-date or pain intensity contrast.
The retrospective rehabilitation study compares motor rating changes by initial apathy. It provides no distinct date exposure or pain-severity comparison.
The CYCLE-II baseline study models movement and nonmotor symptom measures against daily steps. It contains no measured dietary date contrast or pain change due to an intervention.
The prodromal cohort compares activity and cognition or MDS-UPDRS totals. The analysis lacks a date exposure, a dedicated pain outcome and a baseline diagnosis of Parkinson disease.
The genetic cohort's NMSQuest pain item records reported presence of pain. The group differences reflect genetic associations without dried-date intake or a pain intensity response.
The distinct speech clusters are compared on a composite tremor score including rest items. The results do not isolate raw figs or a rest-item response to eating.
Rest tremor appears as disease background. Results concern physical activity and overall ratings in a prodromal cohort, without an assigned raw-fig or individual rest tremor outcome.
Apathy is mentioned in the planned depression, anxiety and stress scale. The dance pilot protocol reports no results or isolated date preparation.
The main comparisons are medication effects and reported wearing-off. A separate apathy change or dietary dried-date comparison was not supplied.
The clinical study assessed baseline apathy before rehabilitation and related it to motor improvement. It did not repeat the apathy measure at discharge or compare consumption of dried dates.
A clinician-rated apathy item is included in a baseline analysis of daily steps. The comparison does not measure a change after dried-date exposure.
The genetic study uses NMSQuest item 13 for apathy. No clear relation to rare variant carrier status is reported for that item, and no date exposure was compared.
